subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A closed Amperian loop is drawn in a region where a current carrying wire passes entirely outside the loop. For this loop:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: the line integral equals μ₀ times that external current
option_b: the line integral is undefined because Ampere's law cannot be applied when a current lies outside
option_c: the line integral of B dot dl is zero, although B is not zero at points on the loop
option_d: both the line integral and the field B are zero at every point of the loop
correct_answer: the line integral of B dot dl is zero, although B is not zero at points on the loop
explanation: The external current produces a magnetic field at every point of the loop, so B is not zero there. However, its circulation around a loop that it does not thread is zero, so the contribution of this current to the line integral vanishes.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A long solid cylindrical conductor of radius 10 cm carries a current of 20 A distributed uniformly. At a point 5 cm from the axis the field has a certain value. The field has the same value at an external point whose distance from the axis is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Find the gyroperiod in the second region
question: An ideal nonrelativistic positively charged particle is accelerated from rest through 1000 V and enters a uniform magnetic field 0.2 T at an unknown angle. Its helical radius is 0.01 m and its advance parallel to the field per turn is 0.06283185307 m. No electric field acts in this region. For a separate second trial, the particle is first brought to rest and then accelerated through 2000 V and enters a second magnetic region of field 0.4 T at the SAME angle. Find the gyroperiod in the second region. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
Geometry gives cotθ=p/(2πr)=1. Since v⊥=(q/m)Br and v²=2(q/m)V, q/m=250000000 C/kg. The second speed is 1000000 m/s and period 6.283185307 × 10⁻⁸ s. Actual path per turn is vT=0.06283185307 m; only the parallel component produces pitch, 0.04442882938 m.
Requested result: 6.283 × 10⁻⁸ s. The object is an ideal charged particle; no atomic-ion species or charge-to-mass restriction is assumed. The second trial starts from rest independently of the first trial. Its kinetic energy on entering the second magnetic region is qV₂, not q(V₁+V₂); magnetic fields do no work.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A coaxial cable has an inner wire carrying 5 A in one direction and an outer cylindrical sheath carrying 5 A in the opposite direction. Find the magnetic field at a point 4 cm from the axis in the gap between the conductors, and at a point 10 cm from the axis outside the cable. Take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: 5 × 10⁻⁵ T in the gap and zero outside
option_b: 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ T in the gap and 1 × 10⁻⁵ T outside
option_c: zero in the gap and 1 × 10⁻⁵ T outside
option_d: 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ T in the gap and zero outside
correct_answer: 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ T in the gap and zero outside
explanation: A circle of radius 4 cm in the gap encloses only the inner current of 5 A, so B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ x 5 / 0.04 = 1 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.04 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ T. A circle of radius 10 cm outside the cable encloses 5 A one way and 5 A the other, so the net enclosed current is zero and B = 0. This confinement of the field is the reason coaxial cables do not radiate.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of the magnetic field taken around any closed path is equal to:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: μ₀ times the net current divided by 2 π r
option_b: μ₀ times the total charge enclosed by the path
option_c: μ₀ times the sum of all currents in the neighbourhood
option_d: μ₀ times the net current passing through the area bounded by that path
correct_answer: μ₀ times the net current passing through the area bounded by that path
explanation: Ampere's law relates the circulation of B around a closed path to the net current threading that path. Currents lying outside the path contribute nothing to the integral, although they do contribute to the field at individual points on the path.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: For a long solid cylindrical conductor of radius R carrying a uniformly distributed current, the magnetic field is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: proportional to 1 / r both inside and outside, with a maximum on the axis
option_b: proportional to r inside, proportional to 1 / r outside, and greatest at the surface
option_d: zero inside and proportional to 1 / r outside
correct_answer: proportional to r inside, proportional to 1 / r outside, and greatest at the surface
explanation: Inside the material the enclosed current grows as r² while the path length grows as r, so B grows linearly with r and is zero on the axis. Outside, the full current is enclosed and B falls as 1 / r. The two expressions meet at r = R, where B = μ₀ I / (2 π R) is the maximum value.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: An Amperian loop encloses steady currents 7 A into the page and 3 A out of it. Another 4 A wire is outside. Find the magnitude of the circulation ∮B·dl. Take μ₀=4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The two enclosed currents are oppositely directed, so the net enclosed current is 7 minus 3 = 4 A. The wire outside contributes nothing. Hence the line integral is 4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 4 = 16 π x 10⁻⁷ T m, that is about 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ T m.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: In applying Ampere's circuital law to a long straight current carrying wire, a circle centred on the wire and lying in a plane perpendicular to it is chosen as the closed path because:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: such a circle is the only closed path for which Ampere's law is valid
option_b: on such a circle the magnitude of B is constant and B is everywhere tangential to the path
option_c: on such a circle B is zero everywhere
option_d: on such a circle B is everywhere perpendicular to the path
correct_answer: on such a circle the magnitude of B is constant and B is everywhere tangential to the path
explanation: Symmetry ensures that B has the same magnitude at every point of the circle and is directed along the tangent, so B dot dl reduces to B dl and the integral becomes B x 2 π r. This makes it possible to solve for B.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: An infinitely long hollow cylindrical conductor carries a cylindrically symmetric steady axial current, with no other magnetic sources. What is the magnetic field in its empty bore?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_b: equal to the value at the outer surface
option_d: zero, because an Amperian loop drawn there encloses no current
correct_answer: zero, because an Amperian loop drawn there encloses no current
explanation: A circular Amperian loop drawn entirely within the hollow region encloses no current, so B x 2 π r = 0 and hence B = 0 everywhere inside the cavity, even though the conductor surrounding it carries a large current.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: At a distant equatorial point r from a short magnetic dipole of moment m, the field magnitude is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The equatorial magnitude is μ₀m/(4πr³), directed opposite to the dipole moment.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: At the ORIGINAL field B1, find the quasistatic external work to move from untwisted to twice the original twist
question: A coil of unknown magnetic moment magnitude μ is suspended on a linear torsion fibre of unknown torsion constant κ. Its untwisted normal is perpendicular to a uniform field. In field 0.3 T it turns through 0.4 radians toward alignment. A separate mechanical calibration with the field off stores 0.001 J in the fibre at twist ξ radians. Use the exact sine/cosine torque law, not the small-angle approximation. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: At the ORIGINAL field B1, the quasistatic external work to move from untwisted to twice the original twist = 0.0002708904369 J. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=0.25 in the units assigned in the stem.
The mechanical calibration gives κ=0.032 N m/rad. Equilibrium requires κθ=μB cosθ, yielding μ=0.04632338894 A m². At twice the twist equilibrium requires B2=0.7932126804 T. In the original field, total potential is κφ²/2−μB1 sinφ, so external work is 0.0002708904369 J and net torque μB1 cosφ−κφ is -0.01591785524 N m.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A bar magnet and a current-carrying solenoid have similar external fields because both behave as:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: A current loop or solenoid has a magnetic dipole moment and the same far-field pattern as a bar magnet.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: According to the Biot Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field dB produced at a point by a small current element I dl depends on the distance r of the point from the element as:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: dB is inversely proportional to r²
option_b: dB does not depend on r
option_c: dB is inversely proportional to r
option_d: dB is directly proportional to r²
correct_answer: dB is inversely proportional to r²
explanation: The Biot Savart law states dB = (μ₀ / 4 π) x I dl sin θ / r². The distance appears as r² in the denominator, so dB falls off as the inverse square of the distance from the current element.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The magnetic field due to a small current element at a point 10 cm away, on the perpendicular to the element, is 2 × 10⁻⁷ T. The field due to the same element at a point 20 cm away, along a line making 30° with the element, is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Doubling the distance from 10 cm to 20 cm reduces the field by a factor of 2² = 4. Changing the angle from 90° to 30° multiplies the field by sin 30 / sin 90 = 0.5. Hence the new field is 2 × 10⁻⁷ x (1 / 4) × 0.5 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ T.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A short current element I dl lies along a straight line. The magnetic field due to this element is zero at points lying:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: on a circle drawn around the element
option_b: on the perpendicular drawn to the element through its midpoint
option_c: on the line along which the element itself is directed
option_d: at every point equally distant from the element
correct_answer: on the line along which the element itself is directed
explanation: The magnitude is dB = (μ₀ / 4 π) x I dl sin θ / r². For points lying along the axis of the element, θ is 0° or 180°, so sin θ = 0 and dB = 0. The field is largest at θ = 90°.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Direction from the right hand rule
question: A current element at the origin points along the positive x direction. The magnetic field due to this element at a point on the positive y axis is directed along:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Here dl is along x_hat and r_hat is along y_hat. The vector product x_hat x y_hat gives z_hat, so the field at that point is along the positive z direction, that is out of the xy plane.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Two identical current elements, each of length 1 cm and carrying 10 A, are placed at the origin, one directed along the positive x axis and the other along the positive y axis. Find the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at a point on the positive z axis, 10 cm from the origin. Take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Each element makes an angle of 90° with the line to the point on the z axis, so each contributes dB = 10⁻⁷ x (10 × 0.01) / (0.10)² = 10⁻⁷ x 0.1 / 0.01 = 1 × 10⁻⁶ T. The element along x gives a field along the negative y direction and the element along y gives a field along the positive x direction, so the two contributions are mutually perpendicular. The resultant is square root of (1 + 1) × 10⁻⁶ = 1.414 × 10⁻⁶ T, that is about 1.4 × 10⁻⁶ T.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The direction of the magnetic field dB produced at a point P by a current element I dl is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: Perpendicular to the plane of dl and the line to P
option_b: along the line joining the element to P
option_c: opposite to the direction of dl
option_d: along the direction of dl itself
correct_answer: Perpendicular to the plane of dl and the line to P
explanation: Because dB involves the cross product dl x r_hat, dB must be perpendicular to both dl and to the position vector r drawn from the element to the point. That is, dB is normal to the plane containing these two vectors.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The vector form of the Biot Savart law for the field of a current element I dl at position vector r from the element is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: dB = (μ₀ / 4 π) x I (dl x r_hat) / r²
option_b: dB = (μ₀ / 4 π) x I (dl x r_hat) / r
option_c: dB = (μ₀ / 4 π) x I (dl . r_hat) / r²
option_d: dB = (μ₀ / 4 π) x I (r_hat x dl) / r²
correct_answer: dB = (μ₀ / 4 π) x I (dl x r_hat) / r²
explanation: The field of an element is a vector perpendicular to both dl and r_hat, so a vector product of dl with r_hat is required, taken in that order, and the magnitude carries an inverse square factor 1 / r².

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Which statement correctly compares the Biot Savart law with Coulomb's law in electrostatics?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: Both are inverse square laws, but the Coulomb field is directed along the line joining the source and the point whereas the Biot Savart field is perpendicular to that line
option_b: Both are inverse square laws and in both cases the field lies along the line joining the source and the point
option_c: Coulomb's law depends on the angular position of the point while the Biot Savart law does not
option_d: The Biot Savart law is an inverse law while Coulomb's law is an inverse square law
correct_answer: Both are inverse square laws, but the Coulomb field is directed along the line joining the source and the point whereas the Biot Savart field is perpendicular to that line
explanation: Both laws vary as 1 / r² and both are linear in their sources. The Coulomb field of a point charge is central, directed along the joining line, and has no angular dependence. The Biot Savart field carries a factor sin θ and is perpendicular to the plane of dl and r, so it is not a central field.
