chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Find the gyroperiod in the second region
question: An ideal nonrelativistic positively charged particle is accelerated from rest through 2000 V and enters a uniform magnetic field ξ T at an unknown angle. Its helical radius is 0.02 m and its advance parallel to the field per turn is 0.06283185307 m. No electric field acts in this region. For a separate second trial, the particle is first brought to rest and then accelerated through 8000 V and enters a second magnetic region of field 0.25 T at the SAME angle. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: the gyroperiod in the second region = 7.853981634 × 10⁻⁷ s. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=0.5 in the units assigned in the stem.
Geometry gives cotθ=p/(2πr)=0.5. Since v⊥=(q/m)Br and v²=2(q/m)V, q/m=32000000 C/kg. The second speed is 715541.7528 m/s and period 7.853981634 × 10⁻⁷ s. Actual path per turn is vT=0.5619851785 m; only the parallel component produces pitch, 0.2513274123 m. The object is an ideal charged particle; no atomic-ion species or charge-to-mass restriction is assumed. The second trial starts from rest independently of the first trial. Its kinetic energy on entering the second magnetic region is qV₂, not q(V₁+V₂); magnetic fields do no work.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic material is 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ at 300 K. Assuming the Curie law, its susceptibility at 450 K is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: By the Curie law chi is proportional to 1 / T, so chi_2 = chi_1 × (T₁ / T₂) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ x (300 / 450) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ x (2 / 3) = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A paramagnetic material has susceptibility 4 × 10⁻⁴ at 250 K. Its Curie constant and its susceptibility at 400 K are respectively:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The Curie constant is C = chi T = 4 × 10⁻⁴ x 250 = 0.1 K. At 400 K the susceptibility is chi = C / T = 0.1 / 400 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: For a paramagnetic material obeying the Curie law, a straight line passing through the origin is obtained by plotting:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: susceptibility against the reciprocal of the absolute temperature
option_b: the logarithm of the susceptibility against the absolute temperature
option_c: the reciprocal of the susceptibility against the reciprocal of the absolute temperature
correct_answer: susceptibility against the reciprocal of the absolute temperature
explanation: Writing the Curie law as chi = C x (1 / T) shows that chi is directly proportional to 1 / T. A plot of chi against 1 / T is therefore a straight line through the origin whose slope is the Curie constant. Equivalently, a plot of 1 / chi against T is also a straight line through the origin.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: According to the Curie law, the magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic material is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_b: inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
option_c: inversely proportional to the square of its absolute temperature
option_d: directly proportional to its absolute temperature
correct_answer: inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
explanation: The Curie law states that for a paramagnetic material chi = C / T, with T the absolute temperature and C the Curie constant of the material. Raising the temperature increases the thermal agitation that disturbs the alignment of the dipoles, so the susceptibility falls.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A paramagnetic sample kept in a fixed magnetic intensity has magnetisation 8 A m⁻¹ at 27° celsius. Assuming the Curie law, its magnetisation at 327° celsius in the same magnetic intensity is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K and T₂ = 327 + 273 = 600 K. At fixed magnetic intensity the magnetisation is proportional to 1 / T, so M₂ = 8 × (300 / 600) = 4 A m⁻¹.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: When a diamagnetic specimen is heated, its magnetic susceptibility:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: decreases in inverse proportion to the absolute temperature
option_b: increases in direct proportion to the absolute temperature
option_d: falls abruptly to zero once a certain temperature is crossed
explanation: Diamagnetism arises from a change induced by the field in the orbital motion of paired electrons. This change does not compete with thermal agitation, because there are no permanent dipoles to be disturbed. Hence the diamagnetic susceptibility is practically independent of temperature.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A diamagnetic sample of volume 1 × 10⁻³ m³ and susceptibility -1.5 × 10⁻⁵ is placed in a magnetic intensity of 1 × 10⁵ A m⁻¹. The magnitude of the total magnetic moment induced in it is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: First M = chi H = (-1.5 × 10⁻⁵) × (1 × 10⁵) = -1.5 A m⁻¹. The total moment is then m_net = M V = -1.5 × 1 × 10⁻³ = -1.5 × 10⁻³ A m², whose magnitude is 1.5 × 10⁻³ A m², directed opposite to the applied field.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Find the field magnitude that would give equilibrium at twice the original twist
question: A coil of unknown magnetic moment magnitude μ is suspended on a linear torsion fibre of unknown torsion constant κ. Its untwisted normal is perpendicular to a uniform field. In field 0.2 T it turns through 0.3 radians toward alignment. A separate mechanical calibration with the field off stores 0.0005 J in the fibre at twist 0.2 radians. Use the exact sine/cosine torque law, not the small-angle approximation. Find the field magnitude that would give equilibrium at twice the original twist. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
The mechanical calibration gives κ=0.025 N m/rad. Equilibrium requires κθ=μB cosθ, yielding μ=0.03925318506 A m². At twice the twist equilibrium requires B2=0.463005096 T. In the original field, total potential is κφ²/2−μB1 sinφ, so external work is 6.719690008 × 10⁻⁵ J and net torque μB1 cosφ−κφ is -0.008520589675 N m.
Requested result: 0.463 T.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Find the helical pitch in the second region
question: An ideal nonrelativistic positively charged particle is accelerated from rest through ξ V and enters a uniform magnetic field 0.5 T at an unknown angle. Its helical radius is 0.02 m and its advance parallel to the field per turn is 0.06283185307 m. No electric field acts in this region. For a separate second trial, the particle is first brought to rest and then accelerated through 8000 V and enters a second magnetic region of field 0.25 T at the SAME angle. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: the helical pitch in the second region = 0.2513274123 m. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=2000 in the units assigned in the stem.
Geometry gives cotθ=p/(2πr)=0.5. Since v⊥=(q/m)Br and v²=2(q/m)V, q/m=32000000 C/kg. The second speed is 715541.7528 m/s and period 7.853981634 × 10⁻⁷ s. Actual path per turn is vT=0.5619851785 m; only the parallel component produces pitch, 0.2513274123 m. The object is an ideal charged particle; no atomic-ion species or charge-to-mass restriction is assumed. The second trial starts from rest independently of the first trial. Its kinetic energy on entering the second magnetic region is qV₂, not q(V₁+V₂); magnetic fields do no work.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: For a diamagnetic substance, the magnetisation and the magnetic intensity are:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: oppositely directed, so the susceptibility is negative and very small in magnitude
option_b: similarly directed, so the susceptibility is positive and very small in magnitude
option_c: oppositely directed, so the susceptibility is negative and very large in magnitude
option_d: similarly directed, so the susceptibility is positive and very large in magnitude
correct_answer: oppositely directed, so the susceptibility is negative and very small in magnitude
explanation: An applied field induces atomic moments in a diamagnetic substance that oppose the field, so M points opposite to H and chi = M / H is negative. The induced moments are tiny, so the magnitude of chi is only about 10⁻⁵.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Identical small spheres of a diamagnetic material X and a paramagnetic material Y are released at the same point in a non uniform magnetic field. Then:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: both X and Y move towards the stronger field, X more slowly than Y
option_b: Y moves towards the weaker field while X moves towards the stronger field
option_c: X moves towards the weaker field while Y moves towards the stronger field
option_d: both X and Y move towards the weaker field, Y more slowly than X
correct_answer: X moves towards the weaker field while Y moves towards the stronger field
explanation: The diamagnetic sphere acquires a moment opposing the field, so the force on it drives it towards the region of weaker field. The paramagnetic sphere acquires a moment along the field, so it is drawn towards the region of stronger field. Both forces are feeble because the magnitudes of the susceptibilities are only about 10⁻⁵.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Among bismuth, aluminium, nickel and platinum, the substance that is diamagnetic is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Bismuth is the standard example of a strongly diamagnetic solid; copper, gold, water, lead and silver behave similarly. Aluminium and platinum have unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic, while nickel is ferromagnetic.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: When a specimen is placed in a uniform magnetic field, the lines of the field are found to be pushed out of the specimen, so that the field inside it is slightly weaker than outside. The specimen is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Since the magnetisation of a diamagnetic specimen opposes the applied field, the resultant field inside it is slightly weaker than the applied field, that is B = mu_r B₀ with mu_r slightly less than one. This shows up as a slight expulsion of the lines of the field from the specimen.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A small piece of a diamagnetic substance brought near the pole of a strong magnet is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_c: neither attracted nor repelled by the magnet
explanation: The field of the magnet induces in the diamagnetic sample a magnetic moment directed opposite to itself. A dipole opposing the field is pushed towards weaker field, so the sample is weakly repelled by the pole of the magnet.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Find the actual distance travelled in one turn in the second region
question: An ideal nonrelativistic positively charged particle is accelerated from rest through 1000 V and enters a uniform magnetic field 0.2 T at an unknown angle. Its helical radius is 0.01 m and its advance parallel to the field per turn is 0.06283185307 m. No electric field acts in this region. For a separate second trial, the particle is first brought to rest and then accelerated through 2000 V and enters a second magnetic region of field 0.4 T at the SAME angle. Find the actual distance travelled in one turn in the second region. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
Geometry gives cotθ=p/(2πr)=1. Since v⊥=(q/m)Br and v²=2(q/m)V, q/m=250000000 C/kg. The second speed is 1000000 m/s and period 6.283185307 × 10⁻⁸ s. Actual path per turn is vT=0.06283185307 m; only the parallel component produces pitch, 0.04442882938 m.
Requested result: 0.06283 m. The object is an ideal charged particle; no atomic-ion species or charge-to-mass restriction is assumed. The second trial starts from rest independently of the first trial. Its kinetic energy on entering the second magnetic region is qV₂, not q(V₁+V₂); magnetic fields do no work.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: At 273 K, which of gadolinium, manganese, copper and oxygen is ferromagnetic?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The common ferromagnetic elements are iron, cobalt, nickel and gadolinium, all of which show spontaneous alignment of atomic moments within domains. Manganese and oxygen are paramagnetic and copper is diamagnetic.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: At the ORIGINAL field B1, find the quasistatic external work to move from untwisted to twice the original twist
question: A coil of unknown magnetic moment magnitude μ is suspended on a linear torsion fibre of unknown torsion constant κ. Its untwisted normal is perpendicular to a uniform field. In field 0.2 T it turns through 0.3 radians toward alignment. A separate mechanical calibration with the field off stores 0.0005 J in the fibre at twist 0.2 radians. Use the exact sine/cosine torque law, not the small-angle approximation. At the ORIGINAL field B1, find the quasistatic external work to move from untwisted to twice the original twist. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
The mechanical calibration gives κ=0.025 N m/rad. Equilibrium requires κθ=μB cosθ, yielding μ=0.03925318506 A m². At twice the twist equilibrium requires B2=0.463005096 T. In the original field, total potential is κφ²/2−μB1 sinφ, so external work is 6.719690008 × 10⁻⁵ J and net torque μB1 cosφ−κφ is -0.008520589675 N m.
Requested result: 6.72 × 10⁻⁵ J.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: When an unmagnetised ferromagnetic specimen is placed in an increasing external magnetic field:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: the number of domains increases steadily until the specimen is saturated
option_b: the domains disappear and the atomic moments become randomly oriented
option_c: the domains break up into progressively smaller regions
option_d: domains favourably oriented with respect to the field grow at the expense of the others
correct_answer: domains favourably oriented with respect to the field grow at the expense of the others
explanation: In a weak field the boundaries between domains move so that domains already pointing near the direction of the field grow at the expense of unfavourably oriented ones. In stronger fields the moments of whole domains rotate into the direction of the field. Together these give the very large magnetisation of a ferromagnetic specimen.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Rewinding a fixed length of wire
question: A wire of a certain length carrying a current I is first bent into a single circular turn and then rewound into two turns of half the original radius, the current remaining the same. The magnetic field at the centre in the second case, compared with the first, is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: For one turn of radius R the field is μ₀ I / (2 R). For two turns each of radius R / 2 the field is μ₀ x 2 x I / (2 x R / 2) = 2 μ₀ I / R. Dividing, the second field is 4 times the first. In general, rewinding a fixed length into N turns multiplies the centre field by N².

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Two circular loops, of radii 10 cm and 5 cm, have a common centre but lie in mutually perpendicular planes. Each carries a current of 10 A. Find the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at the common centre. Take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The 10 cm loop gives (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 10) / (2 × 0.10) = 2 π x 10⁻⁵ T, about 6.28 × 10⁻⁵ T. The 5 cm loop gives (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 10) / (2 × 0.05) = 4 π x 10⁻⁵ T, about 1.26 × 10⁻⁴ T. Since the planes are perpendicular, the two axial fields are perpendicular, so the resultant is 2 π x 10⁻⁵ x square root of (1 + 4) = 2 π square root of 5 × 10⁻⁵ T, which is about 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ T.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A wire bent in the form of a semicircle of radius 10 cm carries a current of 4 A. Find the magnetic field at the centre of the semicircle, ignoring the straight lead wires. Take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: A semicircle is half of a full turn, so the field at the centre is half of μ₀ I / (2 R), that is μ₀ I / (4 R). Substituting, B = (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 4) / (4 × 0.10) = (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 4) / 0.40 = 4 π x 10⁻⁶ T, about 1.26 × 10⁻⁵ T.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Which statement about a plane circular current loop is correct?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: A current loop has no magnetic dipole character because it carries no permanent magnet
option_b: The face of the loop from which the current appears anticlockwise behaves as a south pole
option_c: The face of the loop from which the current appears anticlockwise behaves as a north pole
option_d: Both faces of the loop behave as north poles
correct_answer: The face of the loop from which the current appears anticlockwise behaves as a north pole
explanation: Curling the right hand fingers along the current, the thumb points out of the face from which the current looks anticlockwise. The field emerges from that face, so it acts as the north pole, while the other face, where the current looks clockwise, acts as the south pole.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: For a circular current loop of radius R, the ratio of the magnetic field at an axial point distant R from the centre to the field at the centre itself is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Dividing, B_axis / B_centre = R³ / (R² + x²)³⁄². With x = R this becomes R³ / (2 R²)³⁄² = R³ / (2³⁄² R³) = 1 / (2 square root of 2), which is about 0.354.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: At an axial point very far from a circular current loop, so that the distance x is much greater than the radius R, the magnetic field varies as:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: When x is much greater than R, the term R² in the bracket may be neglected, giving B = μ₀ I R² / (2 x³). Writing the magnetic moment as m = I π R², this becomes B = μ₀ x 2 m / (4 π x³), the standard axial field of a magnetic dipole, which falls off as the cube of the distance.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Square loop compared with circular loop
question: The same length of wire carrying the same current is bent once into a circle and once into a square. The ratio of the magnetic field at the centre of the square to that at the centre of the circle is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: For the circle, 2 π R = L gives R = L / (2 π), so B_circle = μ₀ I / (2 R) = π μ₀ I / L. For the square, 4 a = L gives a = L / 4. Each side is a finite wire whose perpendicular distance from the centre is a / 2, and each side subtends 45° on either side of that perpendicular. One side therefore gives (μ₀ I / (4 π x a / 2)) × (sin 45 + sin 45) = (μ₀ I / (2 π a)) x square root of 2. Four sides give B_square = 2 square root of 2 μ₀ I / (π a) = 8 square root of 2 μ₀ I / (π L). Dividing, B_square / B_circle = 8 square root of 2 / pi² = 11.31 / 9.87 = 1.15. The square gives the slightly stronger central field because parts of it lie closer to the centre.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of N turns, radius R, carrying a current I is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Every element of the loop is at the same distance R from the centre and every element makes an angle of 90° with the line to the centre, so the contributions add directly to give B = μ₀ I / (2 R) for one turn, and N times this for N turns.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A wire in the shape of a circular arc of radius R subtending an angle of 60° at its centre carries a current I. The magnetic field at the centre due to this arc is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: An arc of 60° is one sixth of a full circle, so it contributes one sixth of the full loop field: B = (1 / 6) x μ₀ I / (2 R) = μ₀ I / (12 R).

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Axial field from the centre field
question: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius 3 cm is 125 × 10⁻⁶ T. The magnetic field at a point on its axis, 4 cm from the centre, is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Here square root of (3² + 4²) = 5 cm, so the ratio is 3³ / 5³ = 27 / 125. Hence B_axis = 125 × 10⁻⁶ x 27 / 125 = 27 × 10⁻⁶ T.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A circular loop lies in the plane of the paper and carries a current in the anticlockwise sense as seen by the reader. At the centre of the loop the magnetic field is directed:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: along the circumference in the anticlockwise sense
option_c: into the plane of the paper
option_d: out of the plane of the paper, towards the reader
correct_answer: out of the plane of the paper, towards the reader
explanation: Curl the fingers of the right hand along the anticlockwise current; the extended thumb then points out of the paper. Hence the field at the centre, and everywhere on the axis, is directed out of the plane of the loop towards the reader. That face of the loop behaves as a north pole.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Two concentric circular loops of radii R and 2 R lie in the same plane and carry equal currents I in opposite senses. The magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at their common centre is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The inner loop gives μ₀ I / (2 R) and the outer loop gives μ₀ I / (2 × 2 R) = μ₀ I / (4 R). Because the currents circulate in opposite senses, the two axial fields are oppositely directed, so the resultant is μ₀ I / (2 R) minus μ₀ I / (4 R) = μ₀ I / (4 R), in the sense of the inner loop.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Which statement about the magnetic field of a long straight current carrying conductor is correct? Consider points on a circle centred on the wire in a perpendicular plane.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: Both the magnitude and the direction of B are the same at every point of such a circle
option_b: B has constant magnitude but changing direction around such a circle
option_c: The magnitude of B is greatest on the side of the wire towards which the current flows
option_d: B is zero at all points in the plane perpendicular to the wire
correct_answer: B has constant magnitude but changing direction around such a circle
explanation: The magnitude depends only on r, so all points of a given circle have equal field strength. The direction is tangential to that circle, so it rotates continuously as one moves around the circle. This constancy of magnitude with a tangential direction is precisely what makes such a circle a convenient Amperian loop.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The magnetic field at a perpendicular distance r from a very long straight conductor carrying a steady current I is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Integrating the Biot Savart law along an infinite straight wire gives B = μ₀ I / (2 π r). The field falls off as the first power of the distance, not as its square, because contributions come from the whole length of the wire.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Field at the apex of a triangle
question: Two long parallel wires are perpendicular to the plane of the paper and 10 cm apart. Each carries 10 A, one directed out of the paper and the other into the paper. Find the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at a point P which is 10 cm from each wire. Take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Each wire is 0.10 m from P, so each contributes 2 × 10⁻⁷ x 10 / 0.10 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T. Each field is perpendicular to the line joining that wire to P. Since the wires and P form an equilateral triangle and the currents are oppositely directed, the two field vectors turn out to be inclined at 120° to each other. For two equal vectors of magnitude B at 120°, the resultant magnitude is B square root of (1 + 1 + 2 cos 120) = B. Hence the resultant is 2 × 10⁻⁵ T, directed perpendicular to the line joining the two wires.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A long vertical wire carries a current of 20 A vertically upward. The horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field at the place is 4 × 10⁻⁵ T directed towards the north. The resultant horizontal magnetic field is zero at a point that lies (take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: 10 cm to the east of the wire
option_b: 10 cm to the north of the wire
option_c: 10 cm to the west of the wire
option_d: 5 cm to the west of the wire
correct_answer: 10 cm to the west of the wire
explanation: For cancellation the wire must produce a field of 4 × 10⁻⁵ T pointing south. Equating magnitudes, 2 × 10⁻⁷ x 20 / r = 4 × 10⁻⁵, so r = 4 × 10⁻⁶ / 4 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.10 m = 10 cm. For an upward current, the circular field lines run anticlockwise when seen from above, so the field points south only on the western side of the wire. Hence the point is 10 cm to the west.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A long vertical wire carries a current directed vertically upward. At a point due east of the wire, the magnetic field points towards:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Take the current along the upward vertical and the point to the east. The field direction is given by the vector product of the upward direction with the eastward radial direction, which points to the north. Equivalently, curling the right hand fingers around the upward thumb sends the field anticlockwise seen from above, which is northward on the eastern side.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The magnetic lines of force around a long straight current carrying wire are:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: straight lines radiating outward from the wire
option_b: Concentric circles in planes perpendicular to the wire
option_c: straight lines parallel to the wire
option_d: concentric circles lying in planes containing the wire
correct_answer: Concentric circles in planes perpendicular to the wire
explanation: Point the right thumb along the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers then give the sense in which the circular field lines are traced. These circles lie in planes at right angles to the wire, centred on the wire.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
question: Two very long parallel wires in vacuum each carry 1 A and are 1 m apart. Using μ₀≈4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, find their force per unit length.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The force per length is μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)≈2 × 10⁻⁷ N/m. This is a force calculation, not the current SI definition of the ampere, which is based on the fixed elementary charge.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
question: A long horizontal wire of linear mass density 5 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹ floats in equilibrium 1 cm above a second long horizontal wire that carries a current of 100 A. Find the current in the upper wire. Take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and g = 10 m s⁻².
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The upper wire must be pushed upward, so the magnetic force between the wires must be repulsive, which requires the two currents to flow in opposite directions. Equating the repulsive force per unit length to the weight per unit length gives (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 100 x I) / 0.01 = 5 × 10⁻⁴ x 10. The left side is 2 × 10⁻³ I and the right side is 5 × 10⁻³, so I = 2.5 A.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
subtopic: Closed loop in a uniform field
question: A closed current carrying loop of any shape is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The net force on the loop is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: zero only if the loop is circular
option_b: equal to the torque on the loop divided by its area
option_c: B I L, where L is the perimeter of the loop
option_d: zero, because the vector sum of the length elements around a closed loop is zero
correct_answer: zero, because the vector sum of the length elements around a closed loop is zero
explanation: The total force is the sum of I dl x B over the loop. Since B is the same at every point, it can be taken outside, leaving I (sum of dl) x B. The vector sum of the length elements around any closed path is zero, so the net force vanishes for a loop of any shape. A net torque may nevertheless act, which is what makes motors work.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
question: Three long parallel wires A, B and C lie in one plane with AB = BC = 10 cm. They carry currents of 10 A, 20 A and 30 A respectively, all in the same direction. The force per unit length on wire B is (take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Wire A attracts B with (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 10 × 20) / 0.10 = 4 × 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹ towards A. Wire C attracts B with (2 × 10⁻⁷ x 20 × 30) / 0.10 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹ towards C. These pulls are in opposite directions, so the net force per unit length is 1.2 × 10⁻³ minus 4 × 10⁻⁴ = 8 × 10⁻⁴ N m⁻¹, directed towards C.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
question: Two long parallel wires carry currents I1 and I2 and are separated by a distance d. If I1 is doubled and the separation is halved, the force per unit length between them becomes:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The force per unit length is proportional to I1 and inversely proportional to d. Doubling I1 doubles it and halving d doubles it again, so the product of the two factors gives four times the original value.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
question: A wire bent into a semicircle of radius 0.2 m carries a current of 5 A and is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T directed perpendicular to the plane of the semicircle. The force on the semicircular part of the wire is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: In a uniform field the force on a bent conductor depends only on the vector joining its ends, since F = I (sum of dl) x B and the sum of dl is that joining vector. For a semicircle the ends are separated by the diameter, so L_effective = 2 R = 0.4 m. Hence F = 0.4 × 5 × 0.4 = 0.8 N, directed along the perpendicular bisector of the diameter.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
question: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. The wires:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: exert no force on each other
option_b: exert forces on each other directed along their own lengths
explanation: Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other. Applying the rule for the force on a current carrying conductor shows that for currents in the same direction the forces pull the wires together, while for currents in opposite directions they push them apart.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
topic: Force on Conductor and Between Wires
subtopic: Force on a current carrying conductor
question: A straight conductor of length l carrying a current I is placed in a uniform magnetic field B, making an angle θ with the field. The force on it is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: B I l, independent of the orientation of the conductor
option_b: B I l sin θ, and it is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field
option_c: B I l cos θ, and it is zero when the conductor is perpendicular to the field
correct_answer: B I l sin θ, and it is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field
explanation: The force is the vector product I (l x B), of magnitude B I l sin θ. It is greatest when the conductor is at right angles to the field and vanishes when the conductor lies along the field, since then sin θ = 0.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A proton of mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T with a speed of 4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, its velocity making an angle of 60° with the field. The pitch of the resulting helical path is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The component of velocity along the field is v cos 60 = 4 × 10⁵ x 0.5 = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, and this component is unaffected by the field. The period is T = 2 π m / (q B) = 2 π x 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ x 0.2) = 2 π x 5 × 10⁻⁸ = 3.14 × 10⁻⁷ s. The pitch is 2 × 10⁵ x 3.14 × 10⁻⁷ = 6.28 × 10⁻² m, about 6.3 cm.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A positive charge q moves with speed v at angle θ to a uniform magnetic field B. Find the magnetic-force magnitude.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The magnetic force is the vector product q (v x B), whose magnitude is q v B sin θ. It is greatest when the velocity is perpendicular to the field and zero when the velocity is parallel or antiparallel to it.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: In a velocity selector the electric field is 3 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and the magnetic field is 0.06 T, the two being mutually perpendicular and both perpendicular to the beam. The speed of the particles that pass through undeflected is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: For undeflected motion the electric and magnetic forces must balance: q E = q v B, giving v = E / B = (3 × 10⁴) / 0.06 = 5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. The selected speed does not depend on the charge or the mass of the particle.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A positive ion enters normally through the flat face of a region of uniform magnetic field of width d, the field being perpendicular to its velocity. The radius of the circular arc it would describe is r. The ion fails to emerge from the far face if the width d is at least:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Entering normally, the ion turns on a circle whose centre lies on the entry face. The greatest perpendicular distance it can reach from that face is one radius, attained after it has turned through 90°. The condition for emerging is sin θ = d / r with θ less than 90°, that is d less than r. If d is equal to or greater than r, the ion curves back and returns through the face by which it entered.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A proton of mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C moves with a speed of 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.4 T. The radius of its path is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: An electron and a proton with the same kinetic energy enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles to it. Which statement is correct?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: Both describe circles of equal radius because their charges are equal in magnitude
option_b: The proton radius is about 1836 times the electron radius
option_c: The electron describes the larger circle because it is lighter
option_d: The proton describes the larger circle, its radius being about 43 times that of the electron
correct_answer: The proton describes the larger circle, its radius being about 43 times that of the electron
explanation: Writing the momentum in terms of kinetic energy, p = square root of (2 m K), so r = square root of (2 m K) / (q B). For equal K and equal charge magnitude, r is proportional to the square root of the mass. The proton is about 1836 times as massive as the electron, so its radius is larger by the square root of 1836, which is about 43.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A positive charge moves horizontally towards the east in a horizontal magnetic field directed towards the north. The magnetic force on the charge is directed:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Taking east as the first vector and north as the second, the vector product of east with north points vertically upward. Since the charge is positive, the force is along that direction, that is vertically upward.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: Ions pass undeflected through a velocity selector in which the electric field is 2 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and the magnetic field is 0.1 T. They then enter a region of magnetic field 0.2 T at right angles and describe a circle of radius 0.1 m. The mass to charge ratio of the ions is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The selected speed is v = E / B = (2 × 10⁴) / 0.1 = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. In the analysing field, m / q = r B' / v = (0.1 × 0.2) / (2 × 10⁵) = 0.02 / (2 × 10⁵) = 1 × 10⁻⁷ kg C⁻¹.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A charged particle moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled while the field is unchanged, then:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: the period is halved and the radius is doubled
option_b: both the period and the radius are doubled
option_c: the period of revolution is unchanged and the radius of the path is doubled
option_d: the period is doubled and the radius is unchanged
correct_answer: the period of revolution is unchanged and the radius of the path is doubled
explanation: The radius r = m v / (q B) is proportional to the speed, so doubling v doubles r. The period T = 2 π r / v = 2 π m / (q B) contains no v at all, so it is unchanged. The faster particle simply travels around a proportionately larger circle in the same time.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A proton and an alpha particle, starting from rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference and then enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle path to that of the proton path is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Acceleration through V gives v = square root of (2 q V / m), so r = m v / (q B) = square root of (2 m V / q) / B. Hence r is proportional to the square root of m / q. For the alpha particle m is 4 times and q is 2 times those of the proton, so m / q is doubled and r is larger by the square root of 2, about 1.41 times.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Speed and period from the orbit
question: A proton with a charge to mass ratio of 1 × 10⁸ C kg⁻¹ describes a circle of radius 0.1 m in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. Its speed and the time for one revolution are:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: From r = m v / (q B), the speed is v = (q / m) B r = 1 × 10⁸ x 0.4 × 0.1 = 4 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. The period is T = 2 π m / (q B) = 2 π / (1 × 10⁸ x 0.4) = 2 π / (4 × 10⁷) = 1.57 × 10⁻⁷ s, about 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ s. As a check, 2 π r / v = 0.628 / (4 × 10⁶) gives the same period.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A proton of charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C moves with a speed of 5 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at an angle of 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 2 T. The force on it is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A particle of mass m and positive charge q enters a uniform magnetic field B perpendicularly at nonrelativistic speed v. Find its orbit radius.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, so q v B = m v² / r. Cancelling one power of v gives r = m v / (q B). The radius is therefore proportional to the momentum and inversely proportional to the charge and the field.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The work required to rotate a dipole of moment m from parallel to antiparallel to a uniform field B is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: U changes from -mB to +mB, so the required work is 2mB.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A magnetic dipole of moment 0.5 A m² is at 30° to a uniform field of 0.2 T. The torque magnitude is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: The stable orientation of a magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field has its moment:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: U = -m·B is minimum when the dipole moment is parallel to the field.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: With magnetic field, coil area and suspension torsional constant fixed, increasing the number of turns in a moving-coil galvanometer increases its:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Current sensitivity θ/I = NBA/k increases with the number of turns N.

unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

question: A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The series resistance required for a 10 V voltmeter is:

unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The shunt needed for a 1 A ammeter is approximately:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Equal voltage across galvanometer and shunt gives S = I_gG/(I-I_g) ≈ 0.1/0.999 ≈ 0.10 Ω.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

question: A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter by connecting:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: Find the field magnitude that would give equilibrium at twice the original twist
question: A coil of unknown magnetic moment magnitude μ is suspended on a linear torsion fibre of unknown torsion constant κ. Its untwisted normal is perpendicular to a uniform field. In field ξ T it turns through 0.4 radians toward alignment. A separate mechanical calibration with the field off stores 0.001 J in the fibre at twist 0.25 radians. Use the exact sine/cosine torque law, not the small-angle approximation. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: the field magnitude that would give equilibrium at twice the original twist = 0.7932126804 T. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=0.3 in the units assigned in the stem.
The mechanical calibration gives κ=0.032 N m/rad. Equilibrium requires κθ=μB cosθ, yielding μ=0.04632338894 A m². At twice the twist equilibrium requires B2=0.7932126804 T. In the original field, total potential is κφ²/2−μB1 sinφ, so external work is 0.0002708904369 J and net torque μB1 cosφ−κφ is -0.01591785524 N m.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
subtopic: At the original field B1 and twice the original twist, find the signed net torque, positive toward increasing twist
question: A coil of unknown magnetic moment magnitude μ is suspended on a linear torsion fibre of unknown torsion constant κ. Its untwisted normal is perpendicular to a uniform field. In field 0.2 T it turns through 0.3 radians toward alignment. A separate mechanical calibration with the field off stores 0.0005 J in the fibre at twist 0.2 radians. Use the exact sine/cosine torque law, not the small-angle approximation. At the original field B1 and twice the original twist, find the signed net torque, positive toward increasing twist. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation:
The mechanical calibration gives κ=0.025 N m/rad. Equilibrium requires κθ=μB cosθ, yielding μ=0.03925318506 A m². At twice the twist equilibrium requires B2=0.463005096 T. In the original field, total potential is κφ²/2−μB1 sinφ, so external work is 6.719690008 × 10⁻⁵ J and net torque μB1 cosφ−κφ is -0.008520589675 N m.
Requested result: -0.008521 N m.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A paramagnetic sample of susceptibility 3 × 10⁻⁴ is placed in a magnetic intensity of 2 × 10⁴ A m⁻¹. Its magnetisation is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: M = chi H = 3 × 10⁻⁴ x 2 × 10⁴ = 6 × 10⁰ = 6 A m⁻¹. The magnetisation is along the magnetic intensity because the susceptibility is positive.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A paramagnetic sample is magnetised by placing it in a strong magnetic field. When the field is removed:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: it retains a large part of its magnetisation indefinitely
option_b: its magnetisation stays unchanged until the sample is heated
option_c: it loses its magnetisation almost at once, as thermal agitation randomises the dipoles
option_d: its magnetisation reverses in direction and then slowly dies away
correct_answer: it loses its magnetisation almost at once, as thermal agitation randomises the dipoles
explanation: In a paramagnetic sample the alignment of the permanent dipoles is a balance between the aligning torque of the field and the disordering effect of thermal motion. Once the field is removed, only thermal motion is left, so the dipoles return to random directions and the magnetisation disappears almost immediately.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A paramagnetic rod is placed in a uniform magnetic field. Compared with the field outside, the field inside the rod is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: exactly the same, since the rod does not disturb the applied field
option_b: slightly stronger, since the magnetisation adds to the applied field
option_c: slightly weaker, since the magnetisation opposes the applied field
option_d: very much stronger, since the magnetisation is thousands of times the applied field
correct_answer: slightly stronger, since the magnetisation adds to the applied field
explanation: The magnetisation of a paramagnetic rod points along the applied field, so B = μ₀ (H + M) is a little larger than μ₀ H. Since chi is only about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³, the increase is a fraction of a per cent, which is why the field lines are only slightly more crowded inside the rod.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
chapter: Moving Charges and Magnetism; Magnetism and Matter
question: A paramagnetic sample is kept in a fixed magnetic intensity while its temperature is raised. Its magnetisation:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: increases, because the atomic dipoles gain the energy needed to turn towards the field
option_b: decreases, because increased thermal agitation disturbs the alignment of the atomic dipoles
option_c: remains unchanged, because the number of atomic dipoles does not change
option_d: first increases and then falls to zero at a definite transition temperature

question: A paramagnetic sample contains 5 × 10²⁸ atoms per cubic metre, each having a magnetic moment of 2 × 10⁻²³ A m². In a certain field its measured magnetisation is 10 A m⁻¹. The fraction of the atomic dipoles effectively aligned with the field is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

question: Among copper, aluminium, cobalt and bismuth, the substance that is paramagnetic is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: Aluminium has unpaired electrons and so possesses a permanent atomic magnetic moment, which makes it paramagnetic. Platinum, manganese, chromium and oxygen behave in the same way. Copper and bismuth are diamagnetic and cobalt is ferromagnetic.

question: A rod of a paramagnetic material is freely suspended in a uniform magnetic field. In equilibrium it sets itself:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: with its length perpendicular to the direction of the field
option_b: with its length along the direction of the field
option_c: at an angle that depends on the strength of the applied field
option_d: in a direction fixed only by the way it was suspended
correct_answer: with its length along the direction of the field
explanation: The paramagnetic rod acquires a moment along the field. The torque on a magnetic dipole in a field vanishes and is stable when the moment lies along the field, so the rod turns until its length lies along the direction of the field.

question: Which statement about the magnetic field of a long current carrying solenoid is correct?
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: The field well inside is uniform and directed along the axis, while just outside the winding it is very weak
option_b: The field just outside the winding is equal in magnitude to the field inside
option_c: The field inside is directed radially outward from the axis
option_d: The field inside is strongest near the winding and weakest on the axis
correct_answer: The field well inside is uniform and directed along the axis, while just outside the winding it is very weak
explanation: For a long, closely wound solenoid the interior field is uniform, axial and equal to μ₀ n I at all interior points, while the exterior field is very small because the return flux spreads over a large region. This makes a solenoid the practical way of producing a uniform magnetic field.

question: How many turns must be wound on a solenoid of length 1 m carrying a current of 5 A so that the field inside is 4 π x 10⁻³ T? Take μ₀ = 4 π x 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: n = B / (μ₀ I) = (4 π x 10⁻³) / (4 π x 10⁻⁷ x 5) = (10⁴) / 5 = 2000 turns per metre. Since the length is 1 m, the total number of turns required is 2000.

question: The magnetic field inside a long air cored solenoid can be doubled by:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: doubling the radius of the solenoid
option_b: doubling the current while keeping the number of turns per unit length unchanged
option_c: doubling the length of the connecting leads
option_d: doubling the length while keeping the total number of turns and the current unchanged
correct_answer: doubling the current while keeping the number of turns per unit length unchanged
explanation: Since B = μ₀ n I, the interior field is doubled by doubling either the current or the number of turns per unit length. Doubling the length at fixed total turns halves n and therefore halves B, while changing the radius or the leads has no effect.

question: Two long solenoids have the same number of turns per unit length and carry the same current, but the second has twice the radius of the first. The magnetic fields inside them are related as:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

option_b: the field in the wider solenoid is twice that in the narrower one
option_d: the field in the wider solenoid is half that in the narrower one
explanation: The Amperian rectangle used in the derivation gives B L = μ₀ (n L) I, in which the radius never appears. So long as the solenoid is long compared with its diameter, the interior field depends only on n and I, and the two fields are equal.

question: A solenoid carrying a steady current is stretched to twice its original length, the total number of turns and the current remaining unchanged. The magnetic field inside it becomes:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
option_a: one quarter of its original value
explanation: Stretching at constant N doubles L, so n = N / L is halved. Since B = μ₀ n I and I is unchanged, the field is halved.

question: The magnetic field at a point on the axis at one end of a long solenoid, compared with the field at its middle, is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.
explanation: At the middle, turns lie on both sides and contribute fully. At the end, only half the winding lies on one side, so the axial field is halved: B_end = μ₀ n I / 2.

assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

question: A coil of N turns, area A, carrying a current I is placed in a uniform magnetic field B, the normal to its plane making an angle θ with the field. The torque on the coil is:
assumptions: Use steady source currents and vacuum unless specified otherwise. Particle motion is nonrelativistic, with other forces neglected in magnetic-orbit questions. Listed charge magnitudes are positive. Neglect end and demagnetising effects in ideal long-solenoid models.

question: For a coil rotating uniformly in an ideal AC generator, the induced-emf magnitude is greatest when:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

option_c: the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field, so that the flux linked with it is zero
option_d: the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, so that the flux linked with it is maximum
correct_answer: the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field, so that the flux linked with it is zero
explanation: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux, not on the flux. When the plane of the coil lies along the field the flux linkage is momentarily zero, but it is changing at its fastest rate, and the sine term reaches unity so the emf takes its peak value N B A ω.

correct_answer: zero, because the rate of change of current is zero at that instant
explanation: At the peak of the current waveform the slope di/dt is zero, and since v = L di/dt, the voltage across the inductor is zero at that instant. This is exactly the quarter cycle phase difference expressed instant by instant.
