option_b: π/2 with the current lagging the voltage
option_d: π/2 with the current leading the voltage
explanation: Ohm’s law holds instant by instant in a resistor, so i = (e0 / R) sin(ω t) when e = e0 sin(ω t). Both reach zero and reach their maxima at the same instants, giving zero phase difference.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A 100 Ω resistor is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz AC supply. The average power consumed and the number of times per second at which the instantaneous power becomes zero are respectively:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: P_avg = (220)² / 100 = 48400 / 100 = 484 W. The current is zero twice in each cycle, and with 50 cycles per second the instantaneous power becomes zero 2 × 50 = 100 times per second.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: RMS value of a mixed waveform
question: A current i = 3 + 4 sin(ω t) ampere flows through a circuit. The rms value of this current is nearly:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: i² = 9 + 24 sin(ω t) + 16 sin²(ω t). Over a full cycle the mean of sin(ω t) is 0 and the mean of sin²(ω t) is 0.5. Hence mean of i² = 9 + 0 + 8 = 17, so I_rms = √(17) = 4.12 A.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: An AC source has emf e = 100 sin(200 π t) volt. The rms voltage and the frequency of the source are respectively:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: Peak value e0 = 100 V, so e_rms = 100 / 1.414 = 70.7 V. Also ω = 200 π rad/s, so 2 π f = 200 π giving f = 100 Hz.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: In an AC circuit containing an inductance L and a capacitance C, the quantity √(LC) has the same dimensions as:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: frequency, with dimensional formula [M⁰ L⁰ T⁻¹]
option_b: velocity, with dimensional formula [M⁰ L¹ T⁻¹]
option_c: time, with dimensional formula [M⁰ L⁰ T¹]
option_d: angular acceleration, with dimensional formula [M⁰ L⁰ T⁻²]
correct_answer: time, with dimensional formula [M⁰ L⁰ T¹]
explanation: Since ω = 1 / √(LC) and ω has the dimensions of inverse time, √(LC) must have the dimensions of time, that is [M⁰ L⁰ T¹].

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: An alternating voltage e = 200 sin(100 π t) volt starts from zero at t = 0. The time taken by it to reach its peak value for the first time is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: ω = 100 π rad/s gives f = 50 Hz and T = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s. Starting from zero, the sine first reaches its maximum after a quarter period, that is 0.02 / 4 = 0.005 s = 5 milliseconds.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A sinusoidal alternating current has peak value 10 A. Find its average over the positive half-cycle, using π=3.14.
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Average value over a full cycle
question: Over one complete cycle, the average value of a sinusoidal alternating current is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_b: equal to 0.637 times the peak value
option_c: equal to the peak value of the current
option_d: equal to 0.707 times the peak value
explanation: During the first half cycle the current is positive and during the second half cycle it is equally negative, so the areas under the current time graph cancel and the full cycle mean is zero.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: In an induction furnace, a metal placed inside a coil carrying a high frequency alternating current melts because:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: the coil conducts heat to the metal by direct contact
option_b: the metal loses its resistance and therefore becomes hot
option_c: the alternating magnetic field breaks the chemical bonds of the metal
option_d: strong eddy currents induced in the metal dissipate heat within its own body
correct_answer: strong eddy currents induced in the metal dissipate heat within its own body
explanation: The rapidly changing flux induces very large eddy currents throughout the metal. The i² R heating produced by these currents is generated inside the metal itself and is intense enough to raise the metal to its melting point.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The coil of a dead beat galvanometer is wound on a metallic frame so that:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: the frame carries part of the measured current and protects the coil
option_b: the frame stores the electrical energy of the coil for later use
option_c: the frame increases the magnetic field acting on the coil
option_d: eddy currents induced in the frame oppose the motion and bring the coil quickly to rest
correct_answer: eddy currents induced in the frame oppose the motion and bring the coil quickly to rest
explanation: As the coil turns, the flux through the metal frame changes and eddy currents appear in it. By Lenz's law these currents oppose the rotation, dissipating the energy of the oscillation as heat so the pointer settles at its reading without swinging.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Find the terminal current with the third force
question: A conducting rod of length 0.4 m moves on horizontal rails in an unknown uniform perpendicular field B. The circuit resistance is 4 Ω. Mechanical kinetic friction has an unknown constant magnitude f. A horizontal force ξ N gives terminal speed 1 m/s; a second force 10 N gives terminal speed 3 m/s in the same direction. Self-inductance is negligible. A third force 7 N is used under unchanged conditions. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: the terminal current with the third force = 1.732050808 A. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=4 in the units assigned in the stem.
At terminal speed F=f+(B²L²/R)v. The two trials give drag coefficient 3 N s/m and f=1 N, hence B=8.660254038 T. With F3, v=2 m/s, current=1.732050808 A and Joule heat rate=12 W. Charge over distance d follows ∫I dt=BLd/R, giving 2.598076211 C; mechanical frictional heat is separate.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A solid copper plate swinging between the poles of a strong magnet comes to rest very quickly. If deep slots are cut in the same plate, it will:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: swing for exactly the same time, because copper is not magnetic
option_b: come to rest even faster, because the slots make the plate lighter
option_c: swing for a longer time, because the slots reduce the magnetic field between the poles
option_d: swing for a much longer time, because the slots interrupt the eddy current paths
correct_answer: swing for a much longer time, because the slots interrupt the eddy current paths
explanation: In the solid plate large eddy currents circulate and, by Lenz's law, oppose the swing, damping it rapidly. The slots break these wide circulating paths into narrow ones of much higher resistance, so the currents and the retarding force become small and the plate swings for far longer.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The core of a transformer is built from thin sheets insulated from one another in order to:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: break up the paths available to eddy currents and so raise their resistance
option_b: increase the magnetic flux through the core
option_c: prevent the core from becoming permanently magnetised
option_d: make the core lighter and cheaper to manufacture
correct_answer: break up the paths available to eddy currents and so raise their resistance
explanation: Laminations lie parallel to the flux, so they do not obstruct it, but the insulation between them confines each eddy current to a thin sheet. The narrow paths have a much higher resistance, so the induced currents and the heat they produce are greatly reduced.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A coil of 40 turns and area 0.05 m² is held with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.2 T. It is turned through 180° about a diameter in 0.1 s. The average induced emf is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: Flux per turn changes from +B A = 0.2 × 0.05 = 0.01 Wb to -0.01 Wb, so delta(φ) = 0.02 Wb. Then e = 40 × 0.02/0.1 = 8 V.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A coil of 50 turns and total circuit resistance 10 Ω experiences a flux change of 2 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn. The charge that circulates in the circuit is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A magnet follows the same approach path towards a resistive closed coil in two trials, once in a shorter time. The flux changes monotonically by the same amount, resistance is fixed and self-inductance is negligible. Compared with the slow trial, the fast trial has:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: a smaller induced emf but a larger total induced charge
option_b: a larger induced emf and a larger total induced charge
option_c: the same induced emf and the same total induced charge
option_d: a larger induced emf but the same total induced charge
correct_answer: a larger induced emf but the same total induced charge
explanation: The emf is inversely proportional to the time taken, so faster motion gives a larger emf. The charge is q = integral of i dt = N delta(φ)/R, in which the time interval cancels, so the same flux change always circulates the same charge.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A coil of 500 turns and area 1 × 10⁻² m² has its plane perpendicular to a magnetic field that rises steadily from 0.2 T to 0.6 T in 0.4 s. The resistance of the circuit is 10 Ω. The induced current is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A search coil of 100 turns and area 2 × 10⁻³ m² is connected to a circuit of total resistance 10 Ω. When the coil is quickly pulled out of a uniform field with its plane initially perpendicular to the field, a charge of 4 × 10⁻⁴ C flows. The magnetic field is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The negative sign in the relation e = -N d(φ)/dt indicates that:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: energy is lost during the process of induction
option_b: the induced emf is always negative in value
option_c: The induced emf opposes the flux change
option_d: the magnetic flux always decreases with time
correct_answer: The induced emf opposes the flux change
explanation: The minus sign is the mathematical statement of Lenz's law. The induced emf drives a current whose effect opposes the change in flux, so that work must be done to maintain the change and energy is conserved.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A closed metal ring is placed coaxially near a coil. At the instant the current in the coil is switched on and is rising, the ring:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: stays at rest, because the ring carries no source of emf
option_b: is repelled from the coil, its induced current being opposite in sense to the coil current
option_c: is attracted to the coil, its induced current being in the same sense as the coil current
option_d: is repelled from the coil, its induced current being in the same sense as the coil current
correct_answer: is repelled from the coil, its induced current being opposite in sense to the coil current
explanation: While the coil current rises, the flux through the ring rises. The ring opposes this by driving a current in the opposite sense. Antiparallel currents repel, so the ring is pushed away from the coil.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: Lenz's law states that the direction of the induced current is such that it:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: always flows in the clockwise sense when seen from the magnet
option_b: is always in the same direction as the applied magnetic field
option_c: assists the change in magnetic flux that produces it
option_d: opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it
correct_answer: opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it
explanation: The induced current always flows so that its own magnetic effect opposes the change in flux that caused it. This is expressed by the minus sign in e = -N d(φ)/dt.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: When a magnet is pushed towards a closed coil against the opposing magnetic force, the electrical energy that appears in the coil comes from:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: the thermal energy of the surrounding air
option_b: the magnetic energy stored permanently in the bar magnet
option_c: the electric charges already resident in the coil
option_d: the mechanical work done by the agent pushing the magnet
correct_answer: the mechanical work done by the agent pushing the magnet
explanation: The coil opposes the approach, so the agent must do work against that opposition. This mechanical work is converted into electrical energy in the coil and finally into heat, keeping the total energy constant.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: Two coils P and Q are coaxial, with their winding senses viewed from the same side. P carries a steady current. When its switch is opened and its current decreases, the induced current in resistive closed coil Q:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: flows in the same sense as the current that was flowing in P
option_b: reverses its direction twice before dying away
option_c: flows in the sense opposite to that of the current that was flowing in P
option_d: is zero, because coil P no longer carries any current
correct_answer: flows in the same sense as the current that was flowing in P
explanation: As the current in P collapses, the flux through Q falls. Coil Q opposes this fall by trying to maintain the flux, which requires a current in the same sense as the original current in P.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The north pole of a bar magnet is moved towards one face of a closed circular coil. As seen from the magnet, the induced current in that face flows:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: anticlockwise, so that the near face behaves as a south pole
option_b: anticlockwise, so that the near face behaves as a north pole
option_c: clockwise, so that the near face behaves as a south pole
option_d: in no direction, since the magnet does not touch the coil
correct_answer: anticlockwise, so that the near face behaves as a north pole
explanation: The flux towards the coil increases, so the coil opposes the approach by presenting a north pole to the magnet. A face behaves as a north pole when the current in it runs anticlockwise as seen from the side facing the magnet.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The north pole of a bar magnet is pulled away from a closed coil. The coil then:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: neither attracts nor repels the magnet
option_b: attracts the magnet, its near face behaving as a south pole
option_c: repels the magnet, its near face behaving as a north pole
option_d: attracts the magnet, its near face behaving as a north pole
correct_answer: attracts the magnet, its near face behaving as a south pole
explanation: As the magnet recedes the flux linked with the coil decreases, so the induced current acts to maintain it by attracting the magnet. The near face therefore behaves as a south pole for the receding north pole.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
topic: Inferring RLC parameters from phase measurements
subtopic: Find the maximum capacitor energy during resonance
question: An ideal series RLC circuit is driven by a fixed RMS voltage 100 V. At angular frequency 1000 rad/s its current is 2 A and lags voltage by 45°. At half that angular frequency its current is again I but leads by 45°. All component values remain fixed. The supply frequency is then set to resonance. Find the maximum capacitor energy during resonance. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation:
At the first frequency ωL−1/(ωC)=R; at ω/2 the net reactance is −R. The magnitude gives R=35.35533906 Ω. Solving the signed equations gives L=0.07071067812 H and C=2.828427125 × 10⁻⁵ F. Resonance is ω0=707.1067812 rad/s with current 2.828427125 A. VC,rms=141.4213562 V. Maximum energy uses peak voltage √2VC, hence C VC,rms²=0.5656854249 J.
Requested result: 0.5657 J.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Find the circuit’s terminal Joule-heating power with the third force
question: A conducting rod of length 0.5 m moves on horizontal rails in an unknown uniform perpendicular field B. The circuit resistance is 2 Ω. Mechanical kinetic friction has an unknown constant magnitude f. A horizontal force 3 N gives terminal speed 2 m/s; a second force 5 N gives terminal speed 4 m/s in the same direction. Self-inductance is negligible. A third force 6 N is used under unchanged conditions. Find the circuit’s terminal Joule-heating power with the third force. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation:
At terminal speed F=f+(B²L²/R)v. The two trials give drag coefficient 1 N s/m and f=1 N, hence B=2.828427125 T. With F3, v=5 m/s, current=3.535533906 A and Joule heat rate=25 W. Charge over distance d follows ∫I dt=BLd/R, giving 2.121320344 C; mechanical frictional heat is separate.
Requested result: 25 W.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A bar magnet is completely enclosed inside a closed surface. The net magnetic flux through that closed surface is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: zero only if the magnet is placed exactly at the centre of the surface
option_b: zero, because magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops
option_c: equal to the flux through one face of the surface
option_d: positive and proportional to the pole strength of the magnet
correct_answer: zero, because magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops
explanation: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end; every line that enters the closed surface also leaves it. The inward and outward contributions cancel exactly, so the net flux is zero for any position of the magnet inside.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Flux and shape of the loop
question: A closed flexible wire loop of fixed length is held with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The loop is slowly reshaped from a circle into a square without changing the length of the wire. The flux through the loop:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: becomes zero, because a square loop cannot enclose magnetic field lines
option_b: increases, because a square has four sides and therefore a larger area
option_c: decreases, because for a given perimeter a circle encloses the largest area
option_d: remains the same, because the length of the wire is unchanged
correct_answer: decreases, because for a given perimeter a circle encloses the largest area
explanation: For a fixed perimeter P the circle encloses P²/(4 π) which is about 0.0796 P², while the square encloses P²/16 which is 0.0625 P². The area falls, and since B and the orientation are unchanged the flux falls with it.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Flux with a field given in components
question: A 0.2 m by 0.3 m rectangular loop lies in the xy plane and its chosen normal is +z. With B=(0.1i+0.2j+0.5k) T, find its magnetic flux.
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: The loop lies in the xy plane, so its area vector is along z. Area = 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06 m². Only the z component of B contributes, so φ = 0.5 × 0.06 = 0.03 Wb.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A coil of 200 turns and area 5 × 10⁻³ m² is placed in a uniform field of 0.4 T with its normal along the field. The coil is then rotated so that its normal makes 120° with the field. The magnitude of the change in flux linkage is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: Initial linkage = 200 × 0.4 × 5 × 10⁻³ x cos 0 = 0.4 Wb. Final linkage = 0.4 x cos 120 = 0.4 × (-0.5) = -0.2 Wb. The magnitude of the change is 0.4 - (-0.2) = 0.6 Wb.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Flux change on shrinking a loop
question: A flexible circular loop of radius 0.2 m is held with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.5 T. The loop is shrunk until its radius is 0.1 m, the plane staying perpendicular to the field. Take π = 3.14. The magnitude of the change in flux is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: Initial flux = 0.5 × 3.14 × (0.2)² = 0.5 × 3.14 × 0.04 = 6.28 × 10⁻² Wb. Final flux = 0.5 × 3.14 × (0.1)² = 1.57 × 10⁻² Wb. The change has magnitude 6.28 × 10⁻² minus 1.57 × 10⁻² = 4.71 × 10⁻² Wb, a fall to one quarter of the original value.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Flux linkage of a multi turn coil
question: A coil of 50 turns has an area of 4 × 10⁻² m². A uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T makes an angle of 30° with the plane of the coil. The total magnetic flux linked with the coil is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: The field makes 30° with the plane, so it makes 60° with the normal. N φ = 50 × 0.2 × 4 × 10⁻² x cos 60 = 50 × 0.2 × 0.04 × 0.5 = 0.2 Wb.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A rod of length 1 m rotates in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through its midpoint at 20 rad s⁻¹, in a vertical magnetic field of 0.1 T. The emf between the two ends of the rod is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: Each half of length 0.5 m develops an emf of B ω l²/2 = 0.1 × 20 × 0.25/2 = 0.25 V, with the centre at the same polarity relative to both ends. Going from one end to the other, the two equal emfs oppose each other, so the potential difference between the ends is zero although each end differs from the centre by 0.25 V.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A rod slides on fixed rails in a constant magnetic field with a constant total circuit resistance. If the speed of the rod is doubled, the power that must be supplied becomes:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: The emf B l v doubles and the current e/R doubles with it, so the power, being the product of the two, increases by a factor of four.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A rod of length 0.5 m moves at a constant 4 m s⁻¹ on frictionless rails in a field of 0.4 T, the circuit resistance being 0.2 Ω. The power supplied by the external agent is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: e = 0.4 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.8 V and i = 0.8/0.2 = 4 A. The retarding force is F = B i l = 0.4 × 4 × 0.5 = 0.8 N, so P = F v = 0.8 × 4 = 3.2 W, equal to e²/R = 0.64/0.2 = 3.2 W.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The emf induced across the ends of a conductor moving in a magnetic field arises because:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: the moving conductor becomes electrically charged by friction with the air
option_b: the resistance of the conductor changes as it moves
option_c: the magnetic force q v x B pushes the free charges towards one end of the conductor
option_d: the magnetic field exerts a force on the fixed positive ions of the lattice
correct_answer: the magnetic force q v x B pushes the free charges towards one end of the conductor
explanation: Free charges inside the moving rod share its velocity, so each experiences a magnetic force q v x B along the rod. Charges pile up at the ends until the electric field they set up balances this force, and the resulting potential difference is the motional emf B l v.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A vertical conducting rod PQ, with P at the top, moves to the right with velocity v in a uniform magnetic field directed into the plane of the page. The end at higher potential is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: P, because electrons are heavier than protons and settle at the bottom
option_b: Q, because the magnetic force on the free positive charges is directed downward
option_c: neither, because the rod is not part of a closed circuit
option_d: P, because the magnetic force on the free positive charges is directed upward
correct_answer: P, because the magnetic force on the free positive charges is directed upward
explanation: With v to the right and B into the page, the cross product v x B points upward along the rod. Positive carriers are therefore pushed to the top end P, which becomes positive, while the lower end Q is left negative.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Charge circulated as a rod stops
question: A rod of mass 0.1 kg and length 0.4 m starts at 10 m/s on horizontal frictionless conducting rails. A uniform 0.5 T field is perpendicular to the rail plane. The closed circuit has constant positive resistance and negligible self-inductance. With no external drive, find the total charge passing as speed tends to zero.
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: The retarding force is B i l, and its impulse over the whole motion is B l times the integral of i dt, that is B l q. This impulse must remove all the momentum, so B l q = m v and q = (0.1 × 10)/(0.5 × 0.4) = 1/0.2 = 5 C. Note that the resistance does not enter.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The mutual inductance of two given coils will not change if:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: the distance between the coils is increased
option_b: one coil is turned so that its plane becomes perpendicular to the other
option_c: the current in the primary coil is doubled while everything else is fixed
option_d: a soft iron rod is inserted through both coils
correct_answer: the current in the primary coil is doubled while everything else is fixed
explanation: Mutual inductance is the ratio of flux linkage to current. Since the shared flux is itself proportional to the current, the ratio is unchanged when the current is doubled. Separation, orientation and the core material all change the ratio.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is numerically equal to the:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: current in one coil when unit flux is linked with the other
option_b: emf in one coil when a steady current flows in the other
option_c: flux linked with one coil when unit current flows in the other
option_d: flux linked with one coil when unit current flows in the same coil
correct_answer: flux linked with one coil when unit current flows in the other
explanation: Mutual inductance is defined as the flux linkage produced in the secondary coil per unit current in the primary coil, and is measured in henry.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A short coil of small radius is wound at the middle of a long solenoid of larger radius. In the expression for their mutual inductance, the area that appears is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: the cross sectional area of the outer solenoid
option_b: the difference of the two cross sectional areas
option_c: The cross-sectional area of the inner coil
option_d: the sum of the two cross sectional areas
correct_answer: The cross-sectional area of the inner coil
explanation: The uniform field of the long solenoid exists inside it, and the flux linked with the smaller coil is that field multiplied by the smaller of the two areas. By reciprocity the same value of M is obtained whichever coil is treated as primary, so the inner area is the one that enters.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: Two coils of self inductance 2 H and 8 H have a coefficient of coupling of 0.5. They are connected in series so that their fluxes aid each other. The equivalent inductance is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: M = 0.5 x √(2 × 8) = 0.5 × 4 = 2 H. For fluxes that aid each other, L = L1 + L2 + 2M = 2 + 8 + 4 = 14 H.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The coefficient of coupling k between two coils:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: is measured in henry like the mutual inductance
option_b: is always exactly 1 for any two coils placed near each other
option_c: can take any value greater than 1 for coils on an iron core
option_d: is dimensionless: k = |M|/√(L1 L2), with 0 ≤ k ≤ 1
correct_answer: is dimensionless: k = |M|/√(L1 L2), with 0 ≤ k ≤ 1
explanation: The nonnegative coupling magnitude is k=|M|/√(L1 L2), bounded by 0 and 1. Unity denotes ideal complete coupling with no leakage. One directional flux fraction is insufficient: for long coaxial solenoids with outer area four times inner area, all inner flux can link the outer coil while k=1/2. If directional flux-linkage fractions are used, k is their geometric mean.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: For any two coils placed in a fixed relative position, the mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 and that of coil 2 with respect to coil 1 are:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_b: in the ratio of the numbers of turns of the two coils
option_c: equal only if the two coils have the same self inductance
option_d: equal only if the two coils have the same number of turns
explanation: The reciprocity theorem shows that the flux linkage in coil 2 per unit current in coil 1 is exactly equal to the flux linkage in coil 1 per unit current in coil 2, whatever the shapes, sizes or turn numbers of the coils.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: Two coils of self inductance 2 H and 8 H are wound on the same core so that all the flux of one links the other. Their mutual inductance is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: All the flux is shared, so k = 1 and M = √(2 × 8) = √(16) = 4 H.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A steady direct current flows in the primary of a pair of closely coupled coils. The emf induced in the secondary is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: large, because the coupling between the coils is strong
option_b: equal to M times the primary current
option_c: zero, because the current in the primary is not changing
option_d: equal to the primary emf multiplied by the turns ratio
correct_answer: zero, because the current in the primary is not changing
explanation: The induced emf in the secondary depends on the rate of change of the primary current. For a steady direct current dI_1/dt = 0, so no emf is induced however strong the coupling.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: In an AC circuit, the product of the rms voltage and the rms current is called the apparent power. The true average power is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: equal to the apparent power multiplied by sin(φ)
option_c: always larger than the apparent power
option_d: always exactly equal to the apparent power
explanation: The power factor cos(φ) lies between 0 and 1, so the true power V I cos(φ) is at most equal to the apparent power V I, and equals it only when the phase angle is zero.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The power factor of a circuit containing only a pure inductor, and that of a circuit containing only a pure capacitor, are respectively:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by π/2 and in a pure capacitor it leads by π/2. In both cases cos(φ) = cos(π/2) = 0, so neither element consumes average power.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: An AC circuit draws 5 A from a 200 V supply with the current lagging the voltage by 60°. The average power consumed is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

topic: Inferring RLC parameters from phase measurements
question: An ideal series RLC circuit is driven by a fixed RMS voltage 120 V. At angular frequency ξ rad/s its current is 3 A and lags voltage by 45°. At half that angular frequency its current is again I but leads by 45°. All component values remain fixed. The supply frequency is then set to resonance. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: the resonant angular frequency = 565.6854249 rad/s. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=800 in the units assigned in the stem.
At the first frequency ωL−1/(ωC)=R; at ω/2 the net reactance is −R. The magnitude gives R=28.28427125 Ω. Solving the signed equations gives L=0.07071067812 H and C=4.419417382 × 10⁻⁵ F. Resonance is ω0=565.6854249 rad/s with current 4.242640687 A. VC,rms=169.7056275 V. Maximum energy uses peak voltage √2VC, hence C VC,rms²=1.272792206 J.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Find the charge crossing a circuit section during a further 3 m displacement after terminal motion has been reached
question: A conducting rod of length 0.5 m moves on horizontal rails in an unknown uniform perpendicular field B. The circuit resistance is 2 Ω. Mechanical kinetic friction has an unknown constant magnitude f. A horizontal force 3 N gives terminal speed 2 m/s; a second force 5 N gives terminal speed 4 m/s in the same direction. Self-inductance is negligible. A third force 6 N is used under unchanged conditions. Find the charge crossing a circuit section during a further 3 m displacement after terminal motion has been reached. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation:
At terminal speed F=f+(B²L²/R)v. The two trials give drag coefficient 1 N s/m and f=1 N, hence B=2.828427125 T. With F3, v=5 m/s, current=3.535533906 A and Joule heat rate=25 W. Charge over distance d follows ∫I dt=BLd/R, giving 2.121320344 C; mechanical frictional heat is separate.
Requested result: 2.121 C.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A choke coil is used in a fluorescent tube circuit because:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: it reduces the current using inductive reactance while consuming almost no power
option_b: it reduces the current by converting the excess electrical energy into heat
option_c: it converts the alternating supply into direct current for the tube
option_d: it increases the current through the tube at the moment of starting
correct_answer: it reduces the current using inductive reactance while consuming almost no power
explanation: The large inductive reactance limits the current, while the very small resistance makes the power factor nearly zero, so the average power V I cos(φ) dissipated in the choke is almost nil. A resistor doing the same job would waste large amounts of energy as heat.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Find the circuit’s terminal Joule-heating power with the third force
question: A conducting rod of length 0.4 m moves on horizontal rails in an unknown uniform perpendicular field B. The circuit resistance is 4 Ω. Mechanical kinetic friction has an unknown constant magnitude f. A horizontal force 4 N gives terminal speed 1 m/s; a second force ξ N gives terminal speed 3 m/s in the same direction. Self-inductance is negligible. A third force 7 N is used under unchanged conditions. In this arrangement, the following outcome is measured: the circuit’s terminal Joule-heating power with the third force = 12 W. Which listed positive value of ξ is consistent with that outcome?
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation:
Use the coupled physical relations below. The missing input is ξ=10 in the units assigned in the stem.
At terminal speed F=f+(B²L²/R)v. The two trials give drag coefficient 3 N s/m and f=1 N, hence B=8.660254038 T. With F3, v=2 m/s, current=1.732050808 A and Joule heat rate=12 W. Charge over distance d follows ∫I dt=BLd/R, giving 2.598076211 C; mechanical frictional heat is separate.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Power consumed by a choke coil
question: A choke coil of resistance 2 Ω draws 5 A when connected to a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. The power consumed by the coil is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: Z = 200 / 5 = 40 Ω, so the power factor is 2 / 40 = 0.05. The power is P = I² R = 25 × 2 = 50 W, which also equals V I cos(φ) = 200 × 5 × 0.05 = 50 W. The apparent power is 1000 VA, twenty times the true power.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A series LCR circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.2 H and C = 20 microF. The two half power angular frequencies are nearly:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: LC = 0.2 × 20 × 10⁻⁶ = 4 × 10⁻⁶, so √(LC) = 2 × 10⁻³ and the resonant angular frequency is omega_r = 500 rad/s. The bandwidth is R / L = 10 / 0.2 = 50 rad/s. In the narrow-band approximation the two half power points sit symmetrically at omega_r +/- R/(2L), that is 475 rad/s and 525 rad/s. The keyed pair uses the standard symmetric narrow-band approximation about resonance.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
topic: Inferring RLC parameters from phase measurements
question: An ideal series RLC circuit is driven by a fixed RMS voltage 100 V. At angular frequency 1000 rad/s its current is 2 A and lags voltage by 45°. At half that angular frequency its current is again I but leads by 45°. All component values remain fixed. The supply frequency is then set to resonance. Find the resonant angular frequency. Choose the closest value.

explanation:
At the first frequency ωL−1/(ωC)=R; at ω/2 the net reactance is −R. The magnitude gives R=35.35533906 Ω. Solving the signed equations gives L=0.07071067812 H and C=2.828427125 × 10⁻⁵ F. Resonance is ω0=707.1067812 rad/s with current 2.828427125 A. VC,rms=141.4213562 V. Maximum energy uses peak voltage √2VC, hence C VC,rms²=0.5656854249 J.
Requested result: 707.1 rad/s.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A series LCR circuit with R = 20 Ω is connected to a 200 V AC source of adjustable frequency. The maximum current that can be obtained is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: The current is largest at resonance, where Z = R = 20 Ω. Hence I_max = 200 / 20 = 10 A.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The current in a coil of self inductance 0.5 H changes at the steady rate of 4 A s⁻¹. The magnitude of the self induced emf is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: An inductor stores 2 J of energy when it carries 4 A. The current needed for it to store 4.5 J is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: From 2 = (1/2) L (4)² we get L = 4/16 = 0.25 H. Then 4.5 = (1/2) × 0.25 x I² gives I² = 36 and I = 6 A. Equivalently the current scales as the square root of the energy, and 4 x √(4.5/2) = 4 × 1.5 = 6 A.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: For a coil with a non magnetic core, which statement is correct?
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: The self inductance changes sign when the current is reversed
option_b: The self inductance is zero when no current flows, because the flux is then zero
option_c: The self inductance is a constant of the coil even though it is written as the ratio N φ/I
option_d: The self inductance falls as the current is increased, because I appears in the denominator
correct_answer: The self inductance is a constant of the coil even though it is written as the ratio N φ/I
explanation: For a non magnetic core the flux produced by the coil is directly proportional to the current, so the ratio N φ/I is fixed by the geometry and the core alone. It stays the same whether the current is large, small, zero in the limit, or reversed.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A solenoid of self inductance L is stretched to twice its original length, the number of turns and the cross sectional area remaining the same. Its new self inductance is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: With N and A fixed, L is inversely proportional to l. Doubling the length halves the number of turns per unit length, so the field and the flux for a given current are halved and the inductance falls to L/2.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: An ideal inductor of 2 H carries a steady current of 5 A. The emf induced across it is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
explanation: The current is steady, so dI/dt = 0 and the self induced emf is zero, however large the inductance or the current may be. An ideal inductor behaves like a plain wire for a direct current that does not change.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: Two inductors of 4 H and 6 H, with no mutual coupling between them, are connected in parallel. The equivalent inductance is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: The self inductance of a given coil depends on:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_b: the rate at which the current through it changes
option_d: its number of turns, its dimensions and the permeability of its core
correct_answer: its number of turns, its dimensions and the permeability of its core
explanation: The expression for a solenoid contains only the number of turns, the area, the length and the permeability of the core. The current cancels in the ratio N φ/I because the flux is directly proportional to the current.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A current of 2 A in a coil produces a total flux linkage of 0.4 Wb. The self inductance of the coil is:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: Self inductance is often called the inertia of electricity because:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: it keeps the current constant at all times in every circuit
option_b: it converts electrical energy into heat at a steady rate
option_c: it stores charge in the coil in the way a capacitor does
option_d: it opposes any change in the current through the coil, just as mass opposes a change in velocity
correct_answer: it opposes any change in the current through the coil, just as mass opposes a change in velocity
explanation: The self induced emf always opposes the change in current, so a larger inductance makes the current harder to change. This is exactly the role mass plays in mechanics, where a larger mass makes the velocity harder to change.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
question: A series LCR circuit is operating at a frequency at which the capacitive reactance exceeds the inductive reactance. If the supply frequency is now slowly increased, the impedance of the circuit:
assumptions: AC voltages/currents are sinusoidal RMS values unless a waveform or peak value is given. Components are ideal and linear; magnetic-field/rod/rail geometry is mutually perpendicular where the motional-emf formula is invoked. Neglect self-inductance in purely resistive induction loops.
option_a: decreases continuously, since capacitive reactance always falls with frequency
option_b: first decreases, reaches a minimum equal to R, and then increases
option_c: remains unchanged, since the two reactances change by equal amounts
option_d: increases continuously, since inductive reactance always grows with frequency
correct_answer: first decreases, reaches a minimum equal to R, and then increases
explanation: Raising the frequency increases X_L and decreases X_C, so the magnitude of X_L - X_C first shrinks to zero at resonance, where Z = R, and then grows again as X_L overtakes X_C.

subject: Physics
unit: Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents
subtopic: Find the terminal current with the third force
question: A conducting rod of length 0.5 m moves on horizontal rails in an unknown uniform perpendicular field B. The circuit resistance is 2 Ω. Mechanical kinetic friction has an unknown constant magnitude f. A horizontal force 3 N gives terminal speed 2 m/s; a second force 5 N gives terminal speed 4 m/s in the same direction. Self-inductance is negligible. A third force 6 N is used under unchanged conditions. Find the terminal current with the third force. Choose the closest value.

subtopic: Find the time after switching at which the current first becomes 0.75 A in the direction opposite to its original direction.
question: A coil with unknown inductance L and positive resistance r is connected to an ideal 18 V source at t=0 with zero current. The steady current is 3 A, and the current first reaches 1.5 A at time (ln 2)/2 s. At twice that time, a switch instantaneously reverses the source polarity and inserts an extra 6 Ω in series. The coil current is continuous at switching and the circuit remains closed. Inductance is constant. Find the time after switching at which the current first becomes 0.75 A in the direction opposite to its original direction. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use the idealisations, constants, geometry and sign conventions stated in this question. Any accompanying drawing is schematic.
explanation: The original steady state gives r=18/3=6 Ω. Half-growth takes (L/r)ln2=(ln2)/2, so L=3 H. At twice that time the initial-direction current is 3(1−1/4)=2.25 A. After switching, total resistance is 12 Ω and the signed steady current is −18/12=−1.5 A. Hence I=−1.5+3.75 exp(−4τ). Setting I=−0.75 gives exp(−4τ)=1/5, so τ=(ln5)/4 s. The zero crossing occurs earlier.

subtopic: Find the time after reconnection for the current to reach 1.25 A, in ms.
question: A coil with unknown positive resistance r and inductance L has reached steady current from an ideal 18 V source. Its stored magnetic energy is 6.75 J. In a calibration decay, the source is removed and an extra 6 Ω resistor completes the closed coil loop; the total charge passing through this resistor over the full decay is 0.375 C. In a fresh identical decay, at the instant current falls to 1 A, the 18 V source is reconnected in the original current direction while the extra 6 Ω remains. Switching is ideal and current is continuous. Find the time after reconnection for the current to reach 1.25 A, in ms. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use the idealisations, constants, geometry and sign conventions stated in this question. Any accompanying drawing is schematic.
explanation: Write I₀=18/r. Energy gives (1/2)L(18/r)²=6.75, hence L=r²/24. Total decay charge is I₀L/(r+6)=0.375. Substitution gives 0.75r/(r+6)=0.375, so r=6 Ω and L=1.5 H. After reconnection the final current is 18/12=1.5 A and time constant is 1.5/12=0.125 s. From initial 1 A, I=1.5−0.5 exp(−τ/0.125). The value 1.25 A occurs after 0.125 ln2 s =125 ln2 ms.

subtopic: Find the time after this reconnection at which the current first reaches 0.50 A in the direction opposite to its original direction.
question: A coil of unknown constant inductance L and positive resistance r is connected to an ideal 18 V DC source. Its steady current is 3 A; during the initial growth from zero current, its current is increasing at 4 A/s when it equals 1 A. Once the steady state has been reached, the source is removed and an extra 6 Ω resistor completes the closed coil loop. During this decay, a switch acts when the heat generated in the extra resistor reaches 3 J. It reconnects the 18 V source with polarity opposite to the original current direction, while retaining the extra 6 Ω resistor in series. Switching is ideal, current is continuous, and no other losses occur. Find the time after this reconnection at which the current first reaches 0.50 A in the direction opposite to its original direction. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use the idealisations, constants, geometry and sign conventions stated in this question. Any accompanying drawing is schematic.
explanation: Steady current gives r=18/3=6 Ω. During growth, L(dI/dt)=18−rI gives L=(18−6)/4=3 H. At the start of decay, magnetic energy is (1/2)×3×3²=13.5 J. The coil resistance and extra resistor are equal, so each receives half the dissipated energy; 3 J in the extra resistor means 6 J total loss. Remaining energy is 7.5 J and switching current is √5 A in the original direction. After reconnection, total resistance is 12 Ω, the signed final current is −1.5 A, and L/R=0.25 s. Thus I=−1.5+(√5+1.5)exp(−4t). Setting I=−0.50 gives t=ln(√5+1.5)/4 s. The decay heat must not be treated as the total magnetic-energy loss.

subtopic: Find the mean number of photons absorbed per second
question: A small detector has unknown heat capacity C. A heater of resistance 10 Ω carrying 0.2 A for 20 s raises it by 2 K. After cooling, a plane electromagnetic wave illuminates a detector area 4 cm² for 100 s and raises it by 1 K. The face normal makes 60° with the propagation direction; a fraction 0.5 of the intercepted energy is absorbed. Ignore losses. Use ε0=8.85×10⁻¹² F/m, c=3×10⁸ m/s and photon energy hc/λ with h=6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s and λ=600 nm. Find the mean number of photons absorbed per second. Choose the closest value.
assumptions: Use a plane wave in vacuum unless stated otherwise. Spectrum boundaries are approximate conventional bands, not sharp universal cutoffs; diagrams are schematic.
explanation:
Electrical calibration gives C=4 J/K. The optical absorbed power is 0.04 W. Correct both projected area and absorption to get intensity 400 W/m². Mean intensity is ε0 c E0²/2, so E0=548.9246464 V/m and B0=1.829748821 × 10⁻⁶ T. Absorbed photons per second equal absorbed power divided by hc/λ, 1.206636501 × 10¹⁷ s⁻¹.
Requested result: 1.207 × 10¹⁷ s⁻¹.

question: Compare ideal interference from two equally illuminated, negligibly narrow slits near the centre with Fraunhofer diffraction from one finite slit. Which description is correct?
assumptions: Use paraxial geometrical optics, thin lenses in air and small diffraction/interference angles unless specified otherwise. Sources in path-difference questions are coherent, initially in phase and equally polarised. Media are transparent, isotropic and normally dispersive.
option_a: In interference the bright bands are of equal width and nearly equal brightness, while in diffraction the central band is much wider and much brighter than the rest
option_b: In interference the bands become narrower with order, while in diffraction all bands are of equal width
option_c: Interference occurs only with white light while diffraction occurs only with monochromatic light
option_d: Interference needs a single wavefront while diffraction needs two separate coherent sources
correct_answer: In interference the bright bands are of equal width and nearly equal brightness, while in diffraction the central band is much wider and much brighter than the rest
explanation: In two slit interference the maxima satisfy y = n x λ x D / d, so consecutive bands are equally spaced and of comparable intensity. In single slit diffraction the minima satisfy y = n x λ x D / a, so the central band spans twice the spacing of the others and carries most of the energy.
